V. Adverse Effects Which Cannot Be Avoided
Historically, lands administered by the Bureau of Land Management have generally been open to the use of ORVs. Exceptions to this generality are areas of unique values, which have been closed to ORVs, such as primitive areas, natural areas, and areas of critical wildlife values. On the other hand, lands administered by other Interior bureaus have been closed except where designated open to ORV use. In certain instances, adverse effects will result from ORV use on lands open to such use. However, such effects should be kept at a minimum through the use of regulations developed to control ORV use on Interior lands.
Adverse effects to the proponent user groups include a loss of freedom in areas used.
Non-ORV groups may resent concentration of ORV within certain areas.
Land, water, air, wildlife, and vegetation resources will be detrimentally affected in areas of ORV use.
Noise levels will be discomforting to some users of public lands.
VI. Relationship Between Local Short-Term Uses of Man's Environment and the Maintenance and Enhancement of Long-Term Productivity
Interior Bureaus have major responsibilities for the long-term stewardship of the soil, water, mineral, wildlife, vegetative, and natural and historic resources of the Nation.
An integral part of the proposal, therefore, is the inclusion of periodic review (monitoring) of effects of the proposed action so as to assure that measures taken to satisfy needs of the present do not preclude options for management which must be open to the Department in future years.
At the present, there is a high level of demand for access to the public lands by ORV interests. In recognition of its long-standing concern and responsibility for the recreation interests of the public the Department has proposed an action which will provide for the satisfaction of those interests to the maximum extent commensurate with sound land management and program mission responsibilities of its affected Bureaus.
The current intensifying use of ORV may represent a temporary novelty; on the other hand, it may represent the beginnings of a long-lasting mode of outdoor recreation. The Department's proposed action makes provision for the demands of other rightful users of the public lands; it comprises an attempt to reduce conflicts (for the short run and for the long run) between the two groups of public land users; it initiates monitoring which would disclose the sorts of long-term effects of the action which might threaten resource values of the future.
